The supplied localhost login compares the chosen account's configured password, creates a random token with randomBytes, and stores its user and expiry in a server-side Map. The cookie carries that token. HttpOnly keeps page JavaScript from reading the cookie; SameSite=Strict limits when browsers attach it across sites; Max-Age sets a browser lifetime. The server still verifies its stored expiry. Environment variables supply passwords outside source code. Use your own throwaway local values and do not put them in repository files.

Set the variables in the same terminal where you will start the downloaded local app. In Windows PowerShell, use:
```powershell
$env:ALICE_PASSWORD = "replace-with-a-throwaway-alice-value"
$env:BOB_PASSWORD = "replace-with-a-different-throwaway-bob-value"
```
In a macOS or Linux shell, use:
```bash
export ALICE_PASSWORD="replace-with-a-throwaway-alice-value"
export BOB_PASSWORD="replace-with-a-different-throwaway-bob-value"
```
Replace these example values with different disposable local passwords. These commands set values for that terminal and programs it starts; they do not belong in the source files.

To see what randomBytes produces without printing a token, save this separate example as random-demo.mjs and run it with Node.js:
```javascript
import { randomBytes } from "node:crypto";
const bytes = randomBytes(32);
console.log(bytes.length);
```
The argument 32 requests thirty-two random bytes. With no callback supplied, randomBytes returns a Buffer, a container for bytes. Its length is 32 even though the byte values vary. This prints only the count, not a usable session token. Generating bytes alone does not create a session, associate a user, or enforce expiry.
